# Comparative report: supervised triple‑barrier, regression‑MC optimal stopping, deep optimal‑stopping, and RL/execution approaches for trading exits

## Executive summary
Triple‑barrier supervised labeling (Lopez de Prado) is a practical, path‑dependent labeling scheme widely implemented in production libraries that maps real‑world exit mechanics (profit‑take, stop‑loss, timebar) into training targets and supports meta‑labeling to reduce false positives; it is best for signal-driven classification or hybrid decision‑rules when exit behavior is simple and barriers can be set relative to volatility [1], [2], [6]. Least‑squares Monte‑Carlo (Longstaff & Schwartz) directly estimates continuation value by regression on simulated or historical paths and is the canonical method when an explicit continuation value is needed for stopping decisions; simple linear basis regressions are standard and many open implementations exist [3], [4]. Deep optimal‑stopping approaches (Becker, Cheridito, Jentzen) learn stopping rules using neural networks and Monte Carlo samples and extend classical RMC to high‑dimensional or path‑dependent problems with strong empirical accuracy in the authors’ experiments [5]. The reviewed literature does not include the cited Cont & Kukanov implementations; the closest available work that extends regression‑MC ideas to intervention/control problems is an RMC extension for stochastic impulse control and is recommended as a surrogate reference for execution/liquidation modeling [7].

## 1) Primary sources and code (selected)
Annotated selection of primary materials prioritized in the report:
- Lopez de Prado — triple‑barrier labeling (book chapter implementation context) [1].
- mlfinlab — production implementation of triple‑barrier and meta‑labeling (labeling.py) [2].
- Longstaff & Schwartz — Least‑Squares Monte‑Carlo (original paper) [3].
- longstaff_schwartz GitHub — example LSM implementation [4].
- Becker, Cheridito, Jentzen — Deep Optimal Stopping (JMLR paper) [5].
- Practical note on cost‑aware barrier setting and meta‑labeling effects (author/research summaries) [6].
- RMC extension to stochastic impulse control (closest substitute for Cont & Kukanov execution literature) [7].

(Full URLs appear in References.)

## 2) Labeling and supervised approaches: first‑passage vs triple‑barrier; leakage remedies
Triple‑barrier constructs three path‑dependent boundaries: an upper profit‑taking, a lower stop‑loss, and a vertical timebar; the label is the barrier hit first (e.g., +1/–1/0), and barrier widths are commonly scaled by short‑term volatility estimates so labels reflect execution‑relevant thresholds [1], [2]. Implementations (mlfinlab and community repos) provide utilities to add vertical barriers, compute dynamic target widths, and output binary or ternary labels suitable for classification or for regression targets (e.g., time‑to‑exit or signed return) [2]. Practical remedies to overlapping‑window label leakage (sliding events where multiple events share future price paths) and to side‑conditioning commonly used in industry include meta‑labeling (separating side selection from execution filtering) and careful event construction via event‑centric windows; libraries implement event aggregation and vertical‑barrier mechanics to support this workflow [2], [6].

## 3) Censoring and horizon issues
Triple‑barrier’s vertical bar produces “inconclusive” labels when an episode survives the horizon; implementations record these censored events explicitly so they can be treated as neutral or handled in secondary modeling (meta‑labels) rather than mis‑classifying them as losses or wins [2]. The reviewed sources describe vertical‑barrier handling and meta‑label workflows but do not provide full statistical treatments (e.g., inverse‑probability weighting or survival‑loss functions) in the primary implementations cited; therefore advanced censoring adjustments are not demonstrably standardized in the reviewed code base [1], [2], [6].

## 4) Continuation value and optimal stopping (RMC vs deep)
Longstaff & Schwartz estimate continuation value by regressing realized future cashflows onto basis functions at each backward step; common practice uses low‑dimensional linear bases and Monte‑Carlo sample paths, yielding a tractable stopping rule where stop if immediate payoff ≥ estimated continuation [3], [4]. Deep optimal‑stopping replaces the parametric regression with neural networks that directly learn stop/continue decisions from Monte‑Carlo samples and demonstrated strong accuracy and runtime behavior on high‑dimensional option problems in the JMLR experiments; deep methods are therefore better suited when path dependence or dimensionality makes classical basis expansions ineffective [5]. Extensions that enrich basis sets dynamically (reinforced regression / RMC extensions) are available in the literature as ways to improve classical regression stability and accuracy for intervention problems [7].

## 5) Execution costs, slippage, and market impact
Triple‑barrier labeling can incorporate execution cost considerations by setting horizontal barriers to exceed minimum profit margins needed to clear transaction costs; community and research summaries highlight this practical parameterization approach [6]. The reviewed optimal‑stopping literature (Longstaff & Schwartz; Becker et al.) focuses on valuation/stop decisions from simulated prices and does not prescribe a detailed, standardized market‑impact or partial‑fill model within those primary algorithmic descriptions; extensions to impulse control provide a formalism for modeling interventions but the reviewed sources do not supply a unified production recipe for latency, partial fills, and impact [3], [4], [5], [7].

## 6) Probability outputs, calibration, and diagnostics
The reviewed primary sources and implementations expose classification labels or learned stop/continue decisions but do not document standard calibration pipelines (Platt scaling, isotonic, temperature scaling) or a standardized set of calibration diagnostics in the cited codebases; this is an evidence gap and practitioners must add post‑hoc calibration and reliability diagnostics to convert model scores into actionable exit probabilities [2], [5].

## 7) Overfitting, leakage, nonstationarity, and evaluation protocol
Meta‑labeling and volatility‑scaled barriers are explicit mitigations against overfitting to noise and false positives in supervised labeling workflows [2], [6]. The optimal‑stopping literature improves sample efficiency by using Monte‑Carlo paths and backward induction, with deep methods demonstrating sample efficiency in the published numerical tests but with typical neural‑network caveats (hyperparameter sensitivity) discussed in the deep‑OS paper [5]. The surveyed corpus does not provide a single standardized out‑of‑sample evaluation suite (Sharpe, turnover, execution cost per trade, calibration metrics), so adopting walk‑forward and purged/embargoed splits is recommended in practice though explicit protocols are not enumerated in the cited primary sources [1], [2], [3], [5].

## 8) Limitations and practical recommendations
- Supervised triple‑barrier: best when signals are predictive and exits can be mapped to simple, volatility‑scaled barriers; easy to implement with existing libraries but requires explicit handling of censored/time‑out labels and post‑hoc calibration [1], [2], [6].  
- Regression‑Monte‑Carlo (LSM): preferred when an explicit continuation value is desired and basis functions capture state dependence; mature, interpretable, and supported by simple implementations but limited by basis selection in high dimensions [3], [4].  
- Deep optimal‑stopping: attractive for high‑dimensional or path‑dependent stopping problems; empirically accurate in authors’ tests and scales where LSM basis expansion fails, at cost of neural‑network engineering and hyperparameter tuning [5].  
- RL / execution liquidation: direct Cont & Kukanov materials were not present in the evidence; practitioners should consult RMC extensions for impulse/intervention control as a proximal method and recognize that explicit market‑impact modeling and partial‑fill dynamics must be added outside the primary optimal‑stopping frameworks [7].

Recommended hybrid: use triple‑barrier labeling + meta‑labeling to generate robust supervised signals, use RMC or deep‑OS to estimate continuation/value when a formal stopping policy is needed, and layer an execution model (impact/latency) before live deployment — but implementation specifics require additional sources beyond those cited here.

## Evidence gaps
- No primary Cont & Kukanov papers or official code were available in the provided evidence; an RMC→impulse‑control article is used as the closest substitute [7].  
- No standardized calibration pipelines or concrete calibration diagnostics are provided in the cited primary implementations.  
- No unified, production‑grade treatment of partial fills, execution latency, and detailed market‑impact models is specified in the reviewed sources.

## Reproducibility checklist (minimum actions)
- Obtain and version raw price bars and compute volatility series used for barrier scaling.  
- Use library labeling code (mlfinlab labeling.py) or equivalent to reproduce triple‑barrier labels and vertical‑barrier timestamps [2].  
- For LSM replicate Longstaff & Schwartz backward regression on Monte‑Carlo or historical path samples; example code is available [3], [4].  
- For deep optimal‑stopping follow network/Monte‑Carlo setup in the JMLR paper and reproduce reported experiments before adapting to market data [5].  
- Explicitly store censored/timebar events and document whether they were treated as neutral, excluded, or reweighted (required for reproducibility).  
- Record hyperparameters, random seeds, and data split rules; if using overlapping events adopt a documented embargo/purge policy (not specified in the primary sources).  
Missing information: market‑impact models, calibration pipelines, and Cont & Kukanov primary materials are not present in the evidence and must be sourced separately.

## Works Cited
